title: A Response to “Why Most Unit Testing is Waste”
summary: Rebuttal to Coplien: unit tests earn their keep on algorithmic logic by decoupling design, giving instant feedback and easy context setup, and the usual objections (never-failing tests, refactor breakage, state space) do not hold.

assertions.quote: unit tests are most valuable when you use them for algorithmic logic. They are not particularly useful for code that is more coordinating
I was quite surprised at how much better separated my code become when I started writing unit testing as I was developing.
With unit tests, you get feedback immediately if you make a mistake.
if a unit test fails, it fails as you are developing the code. It is similar to a compilation failure. You fix it immediately.

verdicts.note: Local failures are invisible to repository history so 'never failed' undercounts value, but maintenance cost is real and tests that never fail even locally may be low value.

assertions.quote: Sometimes when you refactor code, you break tests. But my experience is that this is not a big problem.

verdicts.note: Test co-evolution studies show test maintenance is a real and recurring effort, heavily dependent on how mock-heavy and implementation-coupled the tests are.

assertions.quote: This is true, but it applies equally to integration testing, and is thus not an argument against unit testing.

verdicts.note: Both are samples, but a system-level test exercises many units per case, so the argument cuts differently per test.

assertions.quote: it is easier to set up the context you want in a unit test than it is to set it up in the complete system

verdicts.note: Near-definitional and borne out by practice; error-handling paths in particular are hard to trigger end to end.

assertions.quote: Asserts can be useful, but they are not a substitute for unit tests. If an assert fails, there is still a failure

verdicts.note: Assertions do catch what tests missed but after shipping; the two find overlapping faults at different costs.

assertions.quote: Unit tests are not a goal in themselves. They are not useful in every situation.
I agree that integration tests are effective, but I think a combination of both is even better.

verdicts.note: Different test levels find different fault classes, but no study quantifies the marginal catch of adding unit tests to a good integration suite.
